tagline: Rank tracking, site audits and white-label client reports across many projects at once.
verdictSummary: The reporting half is genuinely rebuildable: templated, branded, scheduled PDFs pulling from a database is ordinary work, and it is what agencies actually pay for. The half underneath it is not. Every rank position in those reports is a SERP query against a specific country, language and device, and at agency volumes that is a data bill measured in hundreds of dollars a month whether you subscribe to SE Ranking or to a raw SERP API. Rebuilding the wrapper does not remove the cost.
coreLoopDIY: Track keywords for several client projects through a paid SERP API, store every position history, and generate a branded PDF report per client on a schedule.
whatYouLose: the SERP data itself, which remains a per-query cost at any volume
competitor research and keyword databases built from a proprietary index
the backlink index behind the link-monitoring reports
the site audit crawler and its accumulated rule set
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the subscription is a bulk data contract. An agency tracking two thousand keywords daily is buying SERP queries at a negotiated rate, and the dashboard comes along for free.
notes: The distinguishing angle here is the multi-client reporting layer, not the tracking; the tracking is the part that stays expensive either way.
prompt:
Build a multi-project rank tracker whose real output is a scheduled, branded client report.

Projects: each holds a domain, a set of keywords, a target country, language and device, and a client profile (name, logo, accent colour, contact email). Keywords can carry tags for grouping into report sections.

Data collection: fetch positions through a commercial SERP API whose key sits in the environment, behind a single swappable provider module. Never scrape a search engine directly, and say so in the README. Enforce a daily query budget per project and a global one; when the budget is exhausted, skip and record the skip rather than silently overspending. Store the full raw SERP response for every check, so any reported position can be audited months later, and so a ranking URL change can be explained.

History: positions stored daily with the ranking URL, so URL changes, cannibalisation between two of the client's own pages, and featured-snippet gains are all visible from the same table.

Reporting, which is the reason to build this. A report template composed of blocks the user enables per client: position summary (up, down, unchanged counts), top movers, keywords by tag group with a sparkline each, visibility trend as a weighted score, and a free-text commentary section the operator writes before sending. Render to PDF with the client's logo and colours. Schedule monthly or weekly generation, and email it to the client contact, with every generated report archived so an old one can be reproduced exactly.

Operator views: a dashboard across all projects showing today's biggest movers and any project whose collection failed, plus cost tracking — queries used and estimated spend this month, per project and total. An agency tool that hides its own data bill is useless.

Out of scope: crawling client sites for an audit, backlink data, keyword volume or difficulty estimates, competitor keyword research, and anything requiring a proprietary web index.

faq.q: Can I import my SE Ranking projects and history?
faq.a: Keywords and project settings export as CSV and import cleanly. Position history exports too, but only as a flat table without the ranking URLs, so the historical charts come across while the per-keyword URL history does not.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Dominated by the SERP API. At one to three dollars per thousand queries, tracking 500 keywords daily is roughly 15,000 queries a month, or 15 to 45 dollars, plus a small VPS. That is genuinely cheaper than the Essential plan at that volume, and the gap narrows fast as keyword counts rise.

faq.q: Why not track weekly instead of daily to cut the bill?
faq.a: You can, and for most clients you should — the prompt makes the interval per project for exactly this reason. Daily tracking mainly matters during a migration or a penalty recovery. Weekly cuts the data cost by roughly 85 percent and loses almost nothing in a monthly report.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: The rest of the toolkit. Clients expect the audit, the backlink report and the competitor comparison in the same document, and all three need datasets you cannot buy at this scale. You end up with a very good rank report and nothing to put beside it.
